definition: To make someone appear guilty of a crime or wrongdoing.
example: Muddy paw prints across the sofa incriminated the dog, who sat by the door looking innocent.
nuance: Evidence incriminates by making someone look guilty, while to accuse is to openly blame someone, with or without proof.
prompt: A teacher is trying to find out who scribbled on the classroom whiteboard.
options: Blue ink on her fingertips seemed to incriminate the girl seated by the board.
A hallway video showing him in the library all period served to incriminate the boy completely.
The teacher was careful not to incriminate between neat and messy handwriting when grading.
To thank her for cleaning up, the teacher chose to incriminate the helpful student with a gold star.
reasons: Ink stains are a clue that makes the girl look responsible for the scribbles.
Proof that he was somewhere else clears him, which is the reverse of making him look guilty.
This mixes the word up with discriminate, which means telling things apart.
Giving a reward is praise, but the word only ever points toward guilt.

practice.prompt: Someone ate the last slice of pie at a family picnic.
options: Grandma's confession that she ate the pie herself incriminated the twins and cleared their names.
Dad left the pie in the oven so long that he incriminated the crust to ashes.
Uncle Ray stood up and incriminated that the last slice had been his.
A smear of cherry filling on his chin was enough to incriminate Uncle Ray.
reasons: Someone else's confession takes the blame off the twins instead of putting it on them.
This confuses the word with incinerate, which means to burn something up.
Admitting a fact is not the same thing. Evidence incriminates a person; it isn't a word for confessing.
Leftover filling on his face is evidence that makes him look like the pie thief.
